title: Project Audit
scope: What you looked at and what you left out. Example: security and data handling in `src/`, read-only, no live testing.

findings.title: Password reset links never expire
findings.summary: A reset link works forever once it is sent. Anyone who finds an old email can take over that account.

evidence.excerpt:
const token = await db.resetTokens.find({ value });
if (!token) throw new NotFound();
evidence.note: The lookup checks that the token exists. It never checks `createdAt`.
No code in the auth folder reads an expiry time.

current.description: Reset tokens are random 32-byte values stored in the `reset_tokens` table. A token is deleted when it is used. Nothing else removes it.
pros: Tokens are long and random, so nobody can guess one.
Users who open the email days later can still reset.
cons: An old email in a leaked or shared mailbox still unlocks the account.
The table grows forever because unused tokens are never removed.

coas.name: Expire tokens after one hour
coas.description: Store `expiresAt` with each token and reject it after that time. Delete expired rows in the nightly job.
pros: Closes the takeover path for old emails.
Small change in one file plus one migration.
cons: Users who wait more than an hour must ask for a new link.
coas.recommendedReason: It removes the risk for a tiny cost, and one hour matches what most sites do.

coas.name: Expire tokens when the password changes
coas.description: Delete every open reset token for a user when their password changes by any route.
cons: A leaked link still works until the user happens to change the password.

coas.name: Do nothing
coas.description: Accept the risk and note it in the security docs.

fixFirst.why: Anyone with an old reset email can take over the account.

openQuestions.text: Is one hour too short for users who read email on another device?

notes: Say where your notes are and anything you could not check.
